summary: A surface fungus that coats leaves and young shoots in white powder, slowing growth and, on fruit, causing blemishes.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves and shoots
Leaves curl, pucker or turn yellow and drop
Faint white or russeted patches on fruit
key_sign: White, flour-like powder that wipes off with a finger.
favourable_conditions: Warm days, cool nights and high humidity; unlike most fungi it does not need rain to infect.
spread: Spores spread by wind from infected shoots and leaves; overwinters on buds and fallen leaves.

today: Prune out heavily coated shoot tips and remove them from the orchard
this_week: Apply a fungicide registered for cherry powdery mildew if many leaves are affected
Thin the canopy to improve airflow and sunlight
next_two_weeks: Repeat protection at the label interval during warm, humid weather
Watch fruit as it colours for white patches

chemical: Sulfur-based fungicides, or DMI / QoI fungicides labelled for cherry; rotate groups to avoid resistance
organic: Wettable sulfur (do not use within the label interval of oil sprays)
cultural: Prune for an open, sunny canopy
Avoid excess nitrogen, which produces soft, susceptible growth

prevention: Plant less susceptible varieties where available
Clean up fallen leaves in autumn
